title: DeepSeek's retrained V4-Flash-0731 beats its own 1.6T Pro model on nine agent benchmarks
subtitle: The 284B-parameter MoE model exited preview on July 31 with the same architecture as the April build — every gain came from a new post-training pipeline, and the pricing stays at $0.14 in and $0.28 out per million tokens.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: DeepSeek released DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 as the official production build of its Flash line on July 31, moving the model out of the April public preview. The architecture is unchanged — 284 billion total parameters, 13 billion activated per token via Mixture-of-Experts routing, and a 1-million-token context window. Pricing is $0.14 per million input tokens and $0.28 per million output tokens through the DeepSeek API, and the weights are on Hugging Face under a permissive commercial license. What changed between April and July was the post-training pipeline, not the base model.

The benchmark story is the reason the release is being noticed. On the nine agent-and-coding evaluations DeepSeek published — including Terminal-Bench, SWE-Bench Verified, and Aider polyglot — V4-Flash-0731 outscores DeepSeek's own 1.6-trillion-parameter V4-Pro preview released in April. Terminal-Bench comes in at 82.7%. A model roughly six times smaller than the flagship, and priced at a fraction of it, is winning on the tasks that matter for autonomous agents. The company attributes the gains to reinforcement learning on tool-use trajectories, a new agentic environment corpus, and a redesigned reward model.

The broader signal is where China's open-weight ecosystem sits at the start of Q3. In July alone, Moonshot shipped Kimi K3 to Hugging Face, Meituan released LongCat 2, and Thinking Machines opened Inkling under Apache 2.0. DeepSeek's release closes the month with the sharpest cost-per-capability move so far — a strong agent model at Flash pricing that anyone can run on their own hardware. Frontier US labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) still lead on the very top tier, but the gap between 'the best proprietary model' and 'the best open-weight model you can serve for cents' is measurably narrower than it was at the start of the year.

For learners: the useful lesson from this release is that a lot of remaining AI progress will come from post-training, not from pretraining bigger models. Same weights, better recipe, materially better model. When you evaluate any AI system, ask what training-stage lever is doing the work — architecture, pretraining data, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning, or agent-environment traces. Increasingly the answer for 2026 is the last two. That also means the useful skill for engineers is closer to 'design environments and reward signals' than 'stack more parameters.'
